def generate_disc_cube(
    *,
    field_of_view: u.Quantity,
    pixel_scale: u.Quantity,
    velocity_range: u.Quantity,
    channel_width: u.Quantity,
    beam_size: u.Quantity,
    inc: float,
    pa: float,
    sb_rad: u.Quantity,
    sb_prof: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray,
    vel_rad: u.Quantity,
    vel_prof: u.Quantity,
    gas_sigma: u.Quantity = 0 * u.km / u.s,
    v_sys: u.Quantity = 0 * u.km / u.s,
    redshift: float = 0.0,
    n_clouds: int = 500_000,
    rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
) -> Datacube:
    """Build a KinMS rotating-disc cube in KINO's ``Datacube`` convention.

    Parameters
    ----------
    field_of_view : Quantity (angle)
        Square spatial extent of the output cube.
    pixel_scale : Quantity (angle)
        Spaxel size.
    velocity_range : Quantity (speed)
        Extent of the spectral (velocity) axis.
    channel_width : Quantity (speed)
        Channel width of the spectral axis.
    beam_size : Quantity (angle), scalar
        Circular PSF FWHM to convolve with. Only a circular beam is
        supported by this thin wrapper; pass an elliptical/angled beam
        directly to ``kinms.KinMS`` if needed.
    inc : float
        Inclination, degrees; 0 = face-on, 90 = edge-on (``CLAUDE.md``).
    pa : float
        Position angle, degrees East of North (``CLAUDE.md``); see the
        module docstring for how this maps onto KinMS's ``posAng``.
    sb_rad : Quantity (angle)
        Radius vector for the surface-brightness profile.
    sb_prof : array-like
        Surface-brightness profile (arbitrary scale) vs. ``sb_rad``.
    vel_rad : Quantity (angle)
        Radius vector for the circular-velocity profile.
    vel_prof : Quantity (speed)
        Circular velocity profile vs. ``vel_rad``.
    gas_sigma : Quantity (speed), optional
        Intrinsic (constant) velocity dispersion.
    v_sys : Quantity (speed), optional
        Systemic velocity, added to the spectral axis's zero point.
    redshift : float, optional
        Cosmological redshift recorded on the returned ``Datacube`` as
        metadata only — KinMS itself models in the local/rest frame.
    n_clouds : int, optional
        Number of point-cloud samples (KinMS ``nSamps``); higher reduces
        Monte Carlo noise in the cube at the cost of runtime.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, optional
        Seeded RNG (``CLAUDE.md``: no global RNG use) used to draw a scalar
        seed for KinMS's ``seed`` argument (KinMS internally scales a single
        int into its 4 per-stream seeds -- do not pass a 4-element seed here,
        it silently overflows to an invalid seed for each stream).
        ``None`` uses KinMS's own default seed.

    Returns
    -------
    Datacube
        ``flux`` in arbitrary units (KinMS's default ``Jy/beam``-scaled
        output; no absolute flux calibration is applied). ``spectral_axis``
        is velocity (km/s), linearly spaced and centred on ``v_sys``.
    """
    seed = None
    if rng is not None:
        seed = int(rng.integers(1, 1_000_000))

    model = KinMS(
        xs=field_of_view.to_value(u.arcsec),
        ys=field_of_view.to_value(u.arcsec),
        vs=velocity_range.to_value(u.km / u.s),
        cellSize=pixel_scale.to_value(u.arcsec),
        dv=channel_width.to_value(u.km / u.s),
        beamSize=beam_size.to_value(u.arcsec),
        nSamps=n_clouds,
        seed=seed,
        fixSeed=seed is not None,
        verbose=False,
    )
    cube_xyv = model.model_cube(
        inc=inc,
        posAng=-pa,  # KinMS posAng rotates opposite to KINO's pa -- see module docstring
        gasSigma=gas_sigma.to_value(u.km / u.s),
        sbProf=np.asarray(sb_prof, dtype=float),
        sbRad=sb_rad.to_value(u.arcsec),
        velRad=vel_rad.to_value(u.arcsec),
        velProf=vel_prof.to_value(u.km / u.s),
        vSys=v_sys.to_value(u.km / u.s),
    )
    # KinMS returns (n_x, n_y, n_v); Datacube wants (n_spec, n_y, n_x).
    flux = np.transpose(cube_xyv, (2, 1, 0))

    n_chan = flux.shape[0]
    dv = channel_width.to_value(u.km / u.s)
    spectral_axis = ((np.arange(n_chan) - (n_chan - 1) / 2) * dv + v_sys.to_value(u.km / u.s)) * (
        u.km / u.s
    )

    return Datacube(
        flux=flux,
        spectral_axis=spectral_axis,
        spectral_kind="velocity",
        pixel_scale=pixel_scale.to(u.arcsec),
        redshift=redshift,
        flux_unit=u.dimensionless_unscaled,
        meta={
            "source": "KinMS",
            "citation": "Davis et al. 2013, MNRAS 429, 534",
            "generator_params": {
                "inc_deg": inc,
                "pa_deg": pa,
                "v_sys_kms": v_sys.to_value(u.km / u.s),
                "n_clouds": n_clouds,
            },
        },
    )

docs.title: kino.io.manga
docs.text:
Readers for the real MaNGIA (TNG50 mock MaNGA, Sarmiento et al. 2022) data products, confirmed against live downloads from the TNG-project portal this session (2026-10-21) -- see kino.io.download's module docstring for where/how these are fetched.

This replaces an earlier version of this module that assumed a single flux Datacube with FLUX/ERROR/MASK/GAS extensions, written from the mock-generator code's documentation without a real file to check against. That assumption was wrong: MaNGIA is released as two different product types, neither of which matches it:

  • "maps" (:func:read_mangia_maps -> :class:MangiaMaps): already spatially gridded, but as a stack of 41 named 2-D property maps (VEL, DISP, MASS, SFR, metallicity, age, dust, ... -- see MangiaMaps.maps's keys), not a wavelength-indexed flux cube. There is no spectral axis in this product at all.
  • "rss" (:func:read_mangia_rss -> :class:MangiaRSS): a genuine flux-calibrated spectrum per fibre (shape (n_wave, n_fiber), real units, a real wavelength grid) plus each fibre's real sky position -- but not pre-gridded into a cube. :func:regrid_rss_to_cube turns this into a real :class:~kino.io.base.Datacube via a simplified Gaussian-kernel ("drizzle"-like) regridding -- see its own docstring for exactly what it does and doesn't match about the official MaNGA DRP cubing algorithm (Law et al. 2016) or MaNGIA's own generator code (reginasar/TNG_MaNGA_mocks, GPL-3.0), which this does not call or port, only take inspiration from.

File structure, confirmed directly (not from documentation) by downloading real files for ten TNG50-1 galaxies:

maps (maps/TNG50-{snap}-{subhalo}-{view}-{n_fibers}.cube_maps.fits): INTRINSIC_ASSIGNED (primary): shape (41, ny, nx), one 2-D map per TYPE<i> header key (e.g. TYPE2 = VEL) -- simulation ground truth, not a pyPipe3D fit. Header: CD1_1/CD2_2 (pixel scale, degrees), REDSHIFT, PSF (fibre PSF FWHM, arcsec), FOV (arcsec). Other extensions (MASS_PER_AGE_INTR, MASS_PER_AGE_MET_INTR, LUM_PER_AGE_MET_ASSI, and the pyPipe3D-fit SSP/SFH/indices _pyPipe3D_REC extensions) are not parsed by :func:read_mangia_maps -- out of scope for now, add them if a use for them comes up.

rss (RSS/TNG50-{snap}-{subhalo}-{view}-{n_fibers}.cube_RSS.fits): Primary: flux, shape (n_wave=6603, n_fiber), UNITS header says 1E-16 erg/s/cm^2 (assumed per-Angstrom, i.e. the implicit unit is 1e-16 erg/s/cm^2/Angstrom -- the header does not spell out the /Angstrom, so this is still an assumption, just a far better grounded one than the previous version's). Wavelength grid: CRVAL2/ CDELT2 along axis 2 (3749-10352 Angstrom, 1 Angstrom steps for every file checked). Gas emission extension: same shape, gas-only component (primary is assumed total stars+gas, as real MaNGA cubes are). x_ifu/y_ifu: real fibre sky positions, arcsec, not confirmed to follow KINO's East-of-North sky convention -- same caution as the previous version of this module: verify before using orientation from these. Real values: the same 41 TYPE<i>-keyed ground-truth properties as maps' INTRINSIC_ASSIGNED, here per-fibre (shape (41, n_fiber)) instead of per-spaxel -- this is what makes cross-checking :func:regrid_rss_to_cube possible: regrid Real values' VEL/ DISP the same way as flux and compare against the matching maps file's own gridded VEL/DISP for the same galaxy. N_part_fiber: simulation-particle count per fibre, not used here. mass_t/mass_full/light_full (age/metallicity-resolved, per-fibre) are not parsed -- same scope limit as maps.

def read_mangia_maps(path: str | Path) -> MangiaMaps:
    """Read a MaNGIA "maps" FITS file (see module docstring) into a
    :class:`MangiaMaps`."""
    with fits.open(path) as hdul:
        primary = hdul[0]
        header = primary.header
        data = np.asarray(primary.data, dtype=float)
        if data.ndim != 3:
            raise ValueError(f"expected a 3-D INTRINSIC_ASSIGNED HDU, got shape {data.shape}")
        maps = _type_maps(header, data)
        pixel_scale = (0.5 * (abs(header["CD1_1"]) + abs(header["CD2_2"])) * u.deg).to(u.arcsec)
        return MangiaMaps(
            maps=maps,
            pixel_scale=pixel_scale,
            redshift=_redshift(header),
            psf_fwhm=header["PSF"] * u.arcsec,
            fov=header["FOV"] * u.arcsec,
            meta={"source": "MaNGIA maps (Sarmiento et al. 2022)", "path": str(path)},
        )

def read_mangia_rss(path: str | Path) -> MangiaRSS:
    """Read a MaNGIA "rss" FITS file (see module docstring) into a
    :class:`MangiaRSS`."""
    with fits.open(path) as hdul:

            hdul["Real values"].header, np.asarray(hdul["Real values"].data, dtype=float)

        return MangiaRSS(
            wavelength=wavelength,
            flux=flux,
            flux_gas=flux_gas,
            flux_unit=DEFAULT_RSS_FLUX_UNIT,
            x_fiber=np.asarray(hdul["x_ifu"].data, dtype=float) * u.arcsec,
            y_fiber=np.asarray(hdul["y_ifu"].data, dtype=float) * u.arcsec,

docs.text:
Regrid per-fibre values (last axis = fibre) onto a regular (..., ny, nx) grid by a Gaussian-kernel weighted average -- out[..., y, x] = sum_f w_f(x,y) * values[..., f] / sum_f w_f(x,y), w_f(x,y) = exp(-0.5 * dist((x,y),(x_f,y_f))^2 / sigma^2), sigma = kernel_fwhm / 2.3548.

This is a simplified "drizzle"-like regridding, not a reproduction of the real MaNGA DRP cubing algorithm (Law et al. 2016) or MaNGIA's own generator (reginasar/TNG_MaNGA_mocks): it ignores each fibre's finite aperture (treating it as a point sample) and does not conserve flux through any aperture-overlap accounting. It also has no fibre- bundle footprint mask -- the Gaussian kernel has no hard cutoff, so output pixels outside the real fibre coverage still get a (smoothly extrapolated, increasingly unreliable) value rather than being flagged invalid; mask the output to the fibre bundle's own footprint yourself if you need one (e.g. a matching MangiaMaps map's own != 0 footprint, as notebooks/06_mangia_datacube_demo.ipynb and scripts/validate_mangia_regrid.py do). Validated empirically (not by construction) against MaNGIA's own pre-gridded maps product for the same galaxies, within that footprint -- see notebooks/ and tests/io/test_manga.py for the comparison.

def regrid_fibers_to_grid(
    x_fiber: u.Quantity,
    y_fiber: u.Quantity,
    values: np.ndarray,
    *,
    pixel_scale: u.Quantity,
    nx: int,
    ny: int,
    kernel_fwhm: u.Quantity,
    x0: u.Quantity = 0.0 * u.arcsec,
    y0: u.Quantity = 0.0 * u.arcsec,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Regrid per-fibre ``values`` (last axis = fibre) onto a regular
    ``(..., ny, nx)`` grid by a Gaussian-kernel weighted average --
    ``out[..., y, x] = sum_f w_f(x,y) * values[..., f] / sum_f w_f(x,y)``,
    ``w_f(x,y) = exp(-0.5 * dist((x,y),(x_f,y_f))^2 / sigma^2)``,
    ``sigma = kernel_fwhm / 2.3548``.

    This is a simplified "drizzle"-like regridding, **not** a reproduction
    of the real MaNGA DRP cubing algorithm (Law et al. 2016) or MaNGIA's
    own generator (``reginasar/TNG_MaNGA_mocks``): it ignores each fibre's
    finite aperture (treating it as a point sample) and does not conserve
    flux through any aperture-overlap accounting. **It also has no fibre-
    bundle footprint mask** -- the Gaussian kernel has no hard cutoff, so
    output pixels outside the real fibre coverage still get a (smoothly
    extrapolated, increasingly unreliable) value rather than being flagged
    invalid; mask the output to the fibre bundle's own footprint yourself
    if you need one (e.g. a matching ``MangiaMaps`` map's own ``!= 0``
    footprint, as ``notebooks/06_mangia_datacube_demo.ipynb`` and
    ``scripts/validate_mangia_regrid.py`` do). Validated empirically (not
    by construction) against MaNGIA's own pre-gridded ``maps`` product for
    the same galaxies, within that footprint -- see ``notebooks/`` and
    ``tests/io/test_manga.py`` for the comparison.

    Parameters
    ----------
    x_fiber, y_fiber : Quantity (angle), shape (n_fiber,)
    values : numpy.ndarray, shape (..., n_fiber)
    pixel_scale : Quantity (angle)
    nx, ny : int
    kernel_fwhm : Quantity (angle)
    x0, y0 : Quantity (angle), optional
        Grid centre, same convention as ``x_fiber``/``y_fiber``.

    Returns
    -------
    numpy.ndarray, shape (..., ny, nx)
    """
    n_fiber = x_fiber.shape[0]
    if values.shape[-1] != n_fiber:
        raise ValueError(
            f"values' last axis ({values.shape[-1]}) must match the number of fibres ({n_fiber})"
        )
    px = pixel_scale.to_value(u.arcsec)
    xf = x_fiber.to_value(u.arcsec)
    yf = y_fiber.to_value(u.arcsec)
    x_axis = (np.arange(nx) - (nx - 1) / 2.0) * px + x0.to_value(u.arcsec)
    y_axis = (np.arange(ny) - (ny - 1) / 2.0) * px + y0.to_value(u.arcsec)
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x_axis, y_axis)  # (ny, nx)

    sigma = kernel_fwhm.to_value(u.arcsec) / (2.0 * np.sqrt(2.0 * np.log(2.0)))
    dx = xx[..., np.newaxis] - xf[np.newaxis, np.newaxis, :]
    dy = yy[..., np.newaxis] - yf[np.newaxis, np.newaxis, :]
    w = np.exp(-0.5 * (dx**2 + dy**2) / sigma**2)  # (ny, nx, n_fiber)
    w_sum = w.sum(axis=-1)
    w_sum_safe = np.where(w_sum > 0, w_sum, 1.0)

    out = np.einsum("...f,yxf->...yx", values, w) / w_sum_safe
    return np.where(w_sum > 0, out, 0.0)

docs.text:
Fetch-on-demand for the curated test-data subset (TEST_DATA.md Section 4).

:func:fetch_file is the generic, fully-tested core: download a URL to a destination path, verifying a sha256 checksum, skipping the download if already cached. It has no MaNGIA-specific knowledge and needs no credentials to test (see tests/io/test_download.py, which exercises it against a local HTTP server).

MaNGIA access, confirmed against the real TNG-project portal

A free TNG-project API key (https://www.tng-project.org/users/register/) unlocks the real access point, confirmed live this session: MaNGIA (Sarmiento et al. 2022) is not served as one URL per galaxy. /api/TNG50-1/files/ mangia/ lists exactly three bulk tar.gz archives (MANGIA_ARCHIVES below): catalog (~480 KB, a summary table), maps (~37 GB, the per-galaxy stellar-population/kinematic maps -- see kino.io.manga), and rss (~345 GB, raw per-fiber row-stacked spectra, not pre-gridded into a cube). There is no per-galaxy download URL or listing endpoint.

:func:stream_tar_member_names/:func:stream_extract_tar_member are the generic mechanism this requires: both open the remote tar.gz as a streaming file object (urllib.request -> tarfile.open(..., mode="r|gz")) and stop reading as soon as they've found what they need, so pulling one ~35 MB member out of a 37 GB archive never buffers the whole archive to memory or disk. :func:list_mangia_members/ :func:fetch_mangia_member are the MaNGIA-specific convenience wrappers around them. Finding one specific subhalo's member this way still means streaming through the archive until it's reached -- there is no index, so a member late in the archive costs real time/bandwidth regardless; this is a property of the real data product, not something to fix here.

Large data files are never committed to the repo -- see .gitignore and TEST_DATA.md Section 1.

def fetch_file(
    url: str,
    dest: Path,
    *,
    sha256: str | None = None,
    headers: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False,
) -> Path:
    """Download ``url`` to ``dest``, verifying ``sha256`` if given.

    Skips the download (returns immediately) if ``dest`` already exists and
    (when ``sha256`` is given) matches it, unless ``overwrite=True``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the downloaded file's sha256 doesn't match ``sha256``.
    """
    dest = Path(dest)
    if dest.exists() and not overwrite and (sha256 is None or _sha256_of(dest) == sha256):
        return dest

    dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cached_path = download_file(url, cache=False, http_headers=headers, show_progress=False)

    if sha256 is not None:
        digest = _sha256_of(Path(cached_path))
        if digest != sha256:
            raise ValueError(f"checksum mismatch for {url}: expected {sha256}, got {digest}")

    shutil.copy(cached_path, dest)
    return dest

def stream_tar_member_names(
    url: str, *, headers: dict[str, str] | None = None, limit: int | None = None
) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Yield member names of the remote ``.tar.gz`` at ``url``, without
    downloading or extracting any file content.

    Stops reading the remote stream as soon as ``limit`` names have been
    yielded (``None``: read to the end of the archive).
    """
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=headers or {})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp, tarfile.open(fileobj=resp, mode="r|gz") as tf:
        for i, member in enumerate(tf):
            if limit is not None and i >= limit:
                return
            yield member.name

def stream_extract_tar_members(
    url: str,
    members: dict[str, Path],
    *,
    headers: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False,
) -> dict[str, Path]:
    """Extract several named members from the remote ``.tar.gz`` at ``url``
    in **one streaming pass**, writing each to its own destination in
    ``members`` (``{member name: dest path}``).

    Stops reading the remote stream as soon as every requested member has
    been found, so asking for several members scattered through a large
    archive costs one scan, not one per member (the naive per-member
    approach :func:`stream_extract_tar_member` uses, fine for one member
    but wasteful for many -- see module docstring).

    Members whose ``dest`` already exists are skipped (not re-extracted)
    unless ``overwrite=True``, and are not searched for in the stream.

    Returns
    -------
    dict[str, Path]
        ``{member name: dest path}`` for every member actually extracted
        (or already cached) this call -- members not found in the archive
        are simply absent, not an error (callers can diff against
        ``members`` to see what's missing).
    """
    pending = {
        name: Path(dest) for name, dest in members.items() if overwrite or not Path(dest).exists()
    }
    found: dict[str, Path] = {
        name: Path(dest) for name, dest in members.items() if name not in pending
    }
    if not pending:
        return found

    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=headers or {})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp, tarfile.open(fileobj=resp, mode="r|gz") as tf:
        for entry in tf:
            if entry.name not in pending:
                continue
            extracted = tf.extractfile(entry)
            if extracted is None:
                continue  # not a regular file (e.g. a directory entry)
            dest = pending.pop(entry.name)
            dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            with open(dest, "wb") as out:
                shutil.copyfileobj(extracted, out)
            found[entry.name] = dest
            if not pending:
                break
    return found

def stream_extract_tar_member(
    url: str,
    member: str,
    dest: Path,
    *,
    headers: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False,
) -> Path:
    """Extract exactly ``member`` from the remote ``.tar.gz`` at ``url`` to
    ``dest`` (see :func:`stream_extract_tar_members` -- fetching several
    members from the same archive is far cheaper as one call to that
    function than one call each to this one).

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If ``member`` is not found anywhere in the archive (the whole
        archive is streamed through in this case).
    """
    found = stream_extract_tar_members(
        url, {member: Path(dest)}, headers=headers, overwrite=overwrite
    )
    if member not in found:
        raise KeyError(f"{member!r} not found in {url}")
    return found[member]

docs.title: kino.lensing.shear
docs.text:
Reduced-shear coordinate transform and its effect on ellipticity.

Weak-lensing convention (Bartelmann & Schneider 2001; kappa=0, pure shear -- KINO does not model convergence as a free parameter). Pure shear alone still magnifies (see :func:magnification): with kappa=0, reduced shear equals shear exactly, but det(A) = 1 - |g|**2 != 1, so even an unconverged lens changes the observed solid angle -- and therefore total flux -- of the source. The lens Jacobian A = d(beta)/d(theta) maps an observed sky position theta to the source-plane position beta it came from::

A = [[1 - g1,   -g2  ],
     [  -g2,   1 + g1]]
beta = A @ theta

This is the standard ray-tracing direction: to render what an intrinsic (source-plane) model looks like once lensed, evaluate the source model at beta = A @ theta for each observed pixel theta (see kino.lensing.scene.LensedScene).

Ellipticity convention

KINO's complex ellipticity is eps = eps1 + i*eps2, with magnitude eps = (a-b)/(a+b) (CLAUDE.md) and phase 2*phi, phi the position angle measured the standard math way, counter-clockwise from the +x (East) axis -- not directly KINO's own pa (East of North), which runs the opposite sense from North: phi = 90 deg - pa. This module works in (eps1, eps2) / phi throughout; convert to/from kino.galaxy's pa explicitly (see kino.lensing.scene.photometric_ellipticity for a worked example) -- do not assume eps1 = eps*cos(2*pa) directly, that drops the 90-degree offset and comes out with the wrong sign.

For a circular source (eps=0), reduced shear g = g1 + i*g2 produces eps_obs = g exactly -- this is what fixes the sign/orientation of A above (elongation from positive g1 alone is along the +x axis, i.e. phi=0), and is pinned by tests/lensing/test_shear.py::test_circular_source_ellipticity_equals_g.

For a general intrinsic ellipticity, the composition follows the standard Mobius law (Seitz & Schneider 1997): eps_obs = (eps_int + g) / (1 + conj(g) * eps_int). Note this is not well-approximated by the naive sum eps_int + g except when eps_int is small: expanding in g, eps_obs = eps_int + g - eps_int**2 * conj(g) + O(g**2) -- the responsivity term -eps_int**2 * conj(g) is first order in g too and dominates the naive sum's error at small g whenever eps_int != 0 (see tests/lensing/test_shear.py::test_small_shear_linearisation).

def shear_matrix(g1: float, g2: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """The lens Jacobian ``A`` such that ``beta = A @ theta`` (see module docstring)."""

def shear_ellipticity(eps: complex, g1: float, g2: float) -> complex:
    """Apply reduced shear ``(g1, g2)`` to intrinsic complex ellipticity ``eps``."""
    g = complex(g1, g2)
    return (eps + g) / (1.0 + np.conj(g) * eps)

def unshear_ellipticity(eps_obs: complex, g1: float, g2: float) -> complex:
    """Inverse of :func:`shear_ellipticity`: recover the intrinsic ``eps``."""
    g = complex(g1, g2)
    return (eps_obs - g) / (1.0 - np.conj(g) * eps_obs)

Flux magnification mu = 1 / det(A) = 1 / (1 - g1**2 - g2**2).

KINO's forward model conserves surface brightness under lensing (LensedScene just evaluates the source at the delensed coordinate, with no extra factor) -- magnification of the total flux integrated over a fixed observed area emerges automatically from that coordinate change of variables, exactly as it should (Liouville's theorem). Since det(A) = 1 - |g|**2 < 1 for any nonzero reduced shear, mu > 1 always -- pure shear alone magnifies, with no convergence needed. This matters for anything that uses observed flux as if it were the true (unlensed) flux, e.g. an uncorrected Tully-Fisher luminosity.

def magnification(g1: float, g2: float) -> float:
    """Flux magnification ``mu = 1 / det(A) = 1 / (1 - g1**2 - g2**2)``.

    KINO's forward model conserves *surface brightness* under lensing
    (``LensedScene`` just evaluates the source at the delensed coordinate,
    with no extra factor) -- magnification of the *total* flux integrated
    over a fixed observed area emerges automatically from that coordinate
    change of variables, exactly as it should (Liouville's theorem). Since
    ``det(A) = 1 - |g|**2 < 1`` for any nonzero reduced shear, ``mu > 1``
    always -- pure shear alone magnifies, with no convergence needed. This
    matters for anything that uses observed flux as if it were the true
    (unlensed) flux, e.g. an uncorrected Tully-Fisher luminosity.
    """
    return 1.0 / (1.0 - g1**2 - g2**2)

def measure_moments(image: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray):
    """Flux-weighted centroid and second moments of ``image`` sampled at ``(x, y)``.

    Returns ``(xbar, ybar, qxx, qyy, qxy)``.
    """
    flux = np.asarray(image, dtype=float)
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    total = flux.sum()
    xbar = (flux * x).sum() / total
    ybar = (flux * y).sum() / total
    dx = x - xbar
    dy = y - ybar
    qxx = (flux * dx**2).sum() / total
    qyy = (flux * dy**2).sum() / total
    qxy = (flux * dx * dy).sum() / total
    return xbar, ybar, qxx, qyy, qxy

def measure_ellipticity(image: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray):
    """Centroid, complex ellipticity, and semi-axes of ``image`` at ``(x, y)``.

    Returns ``(xbar, ybar, eps1, eps2, a, b)``, with ``eps = eps1 + i*eps2``
    in ``kino.lensing.shear``'s standard-math-angle convention.
    """
    xbar, ybar, qxx, qyy, qxy = measure_moments(image, x, y)
    trace_half = 0.5 * (qxx + qyy)
    diff_half = 0.5 * (qxx - qyy)
    radius = np.hypot(diff_half, qxy)
    a = np.sqrt(trace_half + radius)
    b = np.sqrt(max(trace_half - radius, 0.0))
    eps_mag = (a - b) / (a + b)
    phi = 0.5 * np.arctan2(2.0 * qxy, qxx - qyy)
    eps1 = eps_mag * np.cos(2.0 * phi)
    eps2 = eps_mag * np.sin(2.0 * phi)
    return xbar, ybar, eps1, eps2, a, b

def generate_batch(
    catalogue_path: str | Path, out_dir: str | Path, *, format: str = "fits"
) -> list[Path]:
    """Generate one mock observation per catalogue galaxy, plus a manifest.

    Parameters
    ----------
    catalogue_path : str or Path
        A catalogue YAML (see module docstring; ``kino/config/
        catalogue_example.yaml`` is a documented template).
    out_dir : str or Path
        Directory for the per-galaxy data files and ``manifest.json``
        (created if missing).
    format : {"fits", "hdf5"}, optional
        Output file format, written via :mod:`kino.io.fitsio`/
        :mod:`kino.io.hdf5`.

    Returns
    -------
    list[Path]
        The written per-galaxy data file paths, in catalogue order.
    """
    if format not in _WRITERS:
        raise ValueError(f"format must be one of {sorted(_WRITERS)}, got {format!r}")
    write_cube, write_slit, ext = _WRITERS[format]

    with open(catalogue_path) as f:
        cfg = yaml.safe_load(f)

    instrument = _build_instrument(cfg["instrument"])
    g1 = float(cfg["shear"]["g1"])
    g2 = float(cfg["shear"]["g2"])
    seed = int(cfg["seed"])

    galaxies_cfg = cfg.get("galaxies")
    population_cfg = cfg.get("population")
    if (galaxies_cfg is None) == (population_cfg is None):
        raise ValueError("catalogue must set exactly one of 'galaxies' or 'population'")

    n = len(galaxies_cfg) if galaxies_cfg is not None else int(population_cfg["n"])
    children = np.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n + 1)
    population_rng = np.random.default_rng(children[0])
    noise_seeds = children[1:]

    rows = (
        [dict(row) for row in galaxies_cfg]
        if galaxies_cfg is not None
        else _sample_population(population_cfg, population_rng)
    )

    allowed = _allowed_fields()
    out_dir = Path(out_dir)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    width = max(4, len(str(n - 1)))
    paths: list[Path] = []
    manifest: list[dict] = []
    for i, (row, child_seed) in enumerate(zip(rows, noise_seeds, strict=True)):
        _validate_row(row, allowed)
        galaxy_kwargs = {k: v for k, v in row.items() if k not in _OBSERVATION_FIELDS}
        galaxy = DiscGalaxy(**galaxy_kwargs)
        line_flux = parse_quantity(row["line_flux"])
        line_wavelength = parse_quantity(row["line_wavelength"])
        rng = np.random.default_rng(child_seed)
        int_seed = int(child_seed.generate_state(1)[0] & 0x7FFFFFFF)

        result = simulate_observation(
            galaxy, g1, g2, instrument,
            line_flux=line_flux, line_wavelength=line_wavelength, rng=rng,
            meta={"catalogue": str(catalogue_path), "seed": int_seed},
        )  # fmt: skip

        path = out_dir / f"galaxy_{i:0{width}d}.{ext}"
        if isinstance(result, SlitObservation):
            write_slit(result, path)
        else:
            write_cube(result, path)
        paths.append(path)

        manifest.append(
            {
                "index": i,
                "file": path.name,
                "seed": int_seed,
                "g1": g1,
                "g2": g2,
                "line_flux": str(line_flux),
                "line_wavelength": str(line_wavelength),
                **dataclasses.asdict(galaxy),
            }
        )

    with open(out_dir / "manifest.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(manifest, f, indent=2)

    return paths

def simulate_observation(
    galaxy: DiscGalaxy,
    g1: float,
    g2: float,
    instrument: Instrument,
    *,
    line_flux: u.Quantity,
    line_wavelength: u.Quantity,
    rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
    meta: dict | None = None,
) -> Datacube | SlitObservation:
    """Shear ``galaxy`` and render it through ``instrument``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    galaxy : DiscGalaxy
        The intrinsic (unlensed) disc.
    g1, g2 : float
        Reduced shear applied via :func:`kino.lensing.apply_shear`.
    instrument : Instrument
        An :class:`~kino.instruments.ifu.IFU` or
        :class:`~kino.instruments.slit.SlitSpectrograph`.
    line_flux : Quantity
        Intrinsic (unlensed) line flux, e.g. ``erg / s / cm**2``.
    line_wavelength : Quantity
        Rest-frame line wavelength.
    rng : numpy.random.Generator or None, optional
        ``None`` (default) returns the noiseless expected-count result;
        pass a seeded generator for one noisy realisation.
    meta : dict or None, optional
        Extra provenance merged into the result's ``Datacube.meta`` (e.g.
        an instrument config path or a batch seed) -- galaxy/shear/line
        fields are always included and take precedence on key collision.

    Returns
    -------
    Datacube or SlitObservation
        Whatever ``instrument.observe()`` returns. For a
        ``SlitObservation``, provenance is written to
        ``result.spectrum.meta`` (the only ``Datacube`` it carries).
    """
    scene = apply_shear(galaxy, g1, g2)
    result = instrument.observe(
        scene, line_flux=line_flux, line_wavelength=line_wavelength, rng=rng
    )

    provenance = dict(meta or {})
    provenance.update(asdict(galaxy))
    provenance["g1"] = g1
    provenance["g2"] = g2
    provenance["line_flux"] = str(line_flux)
    provenance["line_wavelength"] = str(line_wavelength)

    cube = result.spectrum if isinstance(result, SlitObservation) else result
    cube.meta.update(provenance)
    return result

def airmass_from_altitude(altitude: u.Quantity) -> np.ndarray:
    """Relative airmass from apparent altitude (Kasten & Young 1989).

    ``X = 1 / [sin h + 0.50572 (h + 6.07995 deg)^-1.6364]`` (``h`` in
    degrees; Kasten & Young 1989, Appl. Opt. 28, 4735). Finite all the way to
    the horizon (X ~ 38), unlike ``sec z``. Returns ``inf`` for targets below
    the horizon (``h <= 0``).
    """
    h = np.atleast_1d(u.Quantity(altitude).to_value(u.deg)).astype(float)
    x = np.full(h.shape, np.inf)
    up = h > 0.0
    x[up] = 1.0 / (np.sin(np.radians(h[up])) + 0.50572 * (h[up] + 6.07995) ** -1.6364)
    return x

def ecliptic_from_sun(coord: SkyCoord, times: Time) -> tuple[u.Quantity, u.Quantity]:
    """Target ecliptic longitude *relative to the Sun* (wrapped to +/-180 deg)
    and ecliptic latitude, as the zodiacal-light model needs.

    Geocentric true-of-date ecliptic. (SkyCalc's own almanac differed from this
    by ~4 deg in longitude for one tested target; see ``kino.observing.skymodel``.)
    """
    frame = GeocentricTrueEcliptic(obstime=times)
    target = coord.transform_to(frame)
    sun = get_sun(times).transform_to(frame)
    lon = ((target.lon - sun.lon + 180 * u.deg) % (360 * u.deg)) - 180 * u.deg
    return lon.to(u.deg), target.lat.to(u.deg)

def moon_state(site: Site, times: Time, coord: SkyCoord | None = None) -> MoonState:
    """Moon illumination, phase angle, altitude and (optionally) separation.

    The phase angle uses the Sun-Moon elongation and the true distances
    (``i = atan2(R_sun sin e, R_moon - R_sun cos e)``); accurate to well under
    a degree, which is far finer than sky-brightness models need.
    """
    # geocentric Sun and Moon for the phase (both in the same frame); the
    # topocentric Moon for altitude and separation from the target
    moon_geo = get_body("moon", times)
    moon = get_body("moon", times, location=site.location)
    sun = get_sun(times)
    elong = sun.separation(moon_geo)
    r_sun, r_moon = sun.distance.to(u.au), moon_geo.distance.to(u.au)
    phase = np.arctan2(r_sun * np.sin(elong), r_moon - r_sun * np.cos(elong))
    altaz = moon.transform_to(AltAz(obstime=times, location=site.location))
    sep = None
    if coord is not None:
        # ``moon`` is in the site's topocentric GCRS frame and ``coord`` (a distant
        # target) is transformed into it, so this is the topocentric separation --
        # the one that matters for scattered moonlight (lunar parallax is ~1 deg).
        # astropy warns that the result can depend on the transform direction; for a
        # target at infinite distance it does not.
        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            warnings.simplefilter("ignore", NonRotationTransformationWarning)
            sep = moon.separation(coord).to(u.deg)
    return MoonState(
        illumination=(1.0 + np.cos(phase)) / 2.0,
        phase_angle=phase.to(u.deg),
        altitude=altaz.alt.to(u.deg),
        separation=sep,
    )

docs.text:
Effective seeing FWHM at an airmass and wavelength.

Standard Kolmogorov scaling from a zenith seeing quoted at reference_wavelength (conventionally 500 nm): the Fried parameter goes as r0 ~ lambda^(6/5) X^(-3/5) and the FWHM as lambda / r0, so

FWHM = FWHM_ref * X^(3/5) * (lambda / lambda_ref)^(-1/5).

An approximation (it ignores the outer scale, which lowers the FWHM at long wavelengths, and dome/instrument seeing); use it to shape a seeing curve, not to predict a single image to better than ~10%.

Source code in kino/observing/conditions.py 
def seeing_at(
    seeing_ref: u.Quantity,
    airmass: float | np.ndarray,
    wavelength: u.Quantity,
    *,
    reference_wavelength: u.Quantity = REFERENCE_WAVELENGTH,
) -> u.Quantity:
    """Effective seeing FWHM at an airmass and wavelength.

    Standard Kolmogorov scaling from a zenith seeing quoted at
    ``reference_wavelength`` (conventionally 500 nm): the Fried parameter
    goes as ``r0 ~ lambda^(6/5) X^(-3/5)`` and the FWHM as ``lambda / r0``, so

        FWHM = FWHM_ref * X^(3/5) * (lambda / lambda_ref)^(-1/5).

    An approximation (it ignores the outer scale, which lowers the FWHM at
    long wavelengths, and dome/instrument seeing); use it to *shape* a
    seeing curve, not to predict a single image to better than ~10%.
    """
    x = np.asarray(airmass, dtype=float)
    if np.any(x < 1.0):
        raise ValueError("airmass must be >= 1")
    if u.Quantity(seeing_ref).value <= 0:
        raise ValueError("seeing_ref must be positive")
    scale = x**0.6 * (u.Quantity(wavelength) / reference_wavelength).decompose().value ** -0.2
    return u.Quantity(seeing_ref).to(u.arcsec) * scale

def target_track(site: Site, coord: SkyCoord, times: Time) -> TargetTrack:
    """Altitude, airmass and parallactic angle of ``coord`` at ``times``."""
    altaz = coord.transform_to(AltAz(obstime=times, location=site.location))
    # hour angle needs the target's RA *of date* (apparent sidereal time is
    # referred to the true equinox of date); J2000 RA would be off by the
    # accumulated precession (~0.3 deg after 25 years).
    of_date = coord.transform_to(TETE(obstime=times))
    lst = times.sidereal_time("apparent", longitude=site.location.lon)
    hour_angle = (lst - of_date.ra).wrap_at(180 * u.deg)
    lat, dec = site.location.lat, of_date.dec
    q = np.arctan2(
        np.sin(hour_angle),
        np.tan(lat) * np.cos(dec) - np.sin(dec) * np.cos(hour_angle),
    )
    return TargetTrack(
        altitude=altaz.alt.to(u.deg),
        azimuth=altaz.az.to(u.deg),
        airmass=airmass_from_altitude(altaz.alt),
        parallactic_angle=q.to(u.deg),
    )

def extinction_coefficient(wavelength: u.Quantity) -> np.ndarray:
    """CTIO extinction coefficient ``k`` (mag per airmass) at ``wavelength``.

    Linear interpolation in wavelength. Raises ``ValueError`` outside
    3200-10870 A rather than extrapolating.
    """
    wave = np.atleast_1d(u.Quantity(wavelength).to_value(u.angstrom)).astype(float)
    lo, hi = CTIO_WAVELENGTH_ANGSTROM[[0, -1]]
    tol = 1e-6  # Angstrom: unit-conversion round-off at the table edges
    if np.any(wave < lo - tol) or np.any(wave > hi + tol):
        raise ValueError(f"wavelength outside the tabulated CTIO range {lo:.0f}-{hi:.0f} A")
    return np.interp(wave, CTIO_WAVELENGTH_ANGSTROM, CTIO_EXTINCTION_MAG_PER_AIRMASS)

def nir_extinction_coefficient(wavelength: u.Quantity) -> np.ndarray:
    """Broadband CTIO J/H/Ks extinction coefficient (mag per airmass) at ``wavelength``.

    No interpolation between bands (see the module docstring): ``wavelength``
    must fall inside one band's own isophotal-bandwidth window. Raises
    ``ValueError`` otherwise, naming the covered windows.
    """
    wave_um = np.atleast_1d(u.Quantity(wavelength).to_value(u.um)).astype(float)
    out = np.full(wave_um.shape, np.nan)
    covered = np.zeros(wave_um.shape, dtype=bool)
    for band in NIR_EXTINCTION_BANDS:
        lo, hi = band.center_um - band.halfwidth_um, band.center_um + band.halfwidth_um
        inside = (wave_um >= lo) & (wave_um <= hi)
        out[inside] = band.mag_per_airmass
        covered |= inside
    if not covered.all():
        bad = np.round(wave_um[~covered], 4)
        windows = ", ".join(
            f"{b.name} {b.center_um - b.halfwidth_um:.3f}-{b.center_um + b.halfwidth_um:.3f} um"
            for b in NIR_EXTINCTION_BANDS
        )
        raise ValueError(
            f"wavelength(s) {bad} um fall outside every covered NIR band ({windows}) -- "
            "no measured broadband extinction there (see the module docstring)"
        )
    return out

def night_window(
    site: Site,
    date: str | Time,
    *,
    sun_altitude_max: u.Quantity = -18.0 * u.deg,
    step: u.Quantity = 5.0 * u.min,
) -> Night:
    """The dark window of the night that *begins* on local evening ``date``.

    ``date`` is a calendar date (``"2026-10-03"``): the evening of that date
    at the site, running into the next morning. The search starts at the
    site's mean solar noon on that date (12h UT minus the longitude in hours)
    and takes the first contiguous stretch with the Sun below
    ``sun_altitude_max`` -- so no timezone or daylight-saving handling is
    needed, and the result is unambiguous across the UT date boundary.

    Parameters
    ----------
    sun_altitude_max : Quantity (angle), optional
        Default -18 deg (astronomical twilight); use -12 deg for nautical.
    step : Quantity (time), optional
        Grid spacing.
    """
    day = Time(date, scale="utc")
    noon = Time(int(day.mjd) + 0.5, format="mjd", scale="utc") - site.longitude.hour * u.hour
    n = int(round((24 * u.hour / step).decompose().value))
    times = noon + np.arange(n) * step

    sun_alt = get_sun(times).transform_to(AltAz(obstime=times, location=site.location)).alt
    dark = sun_alt < sun_altitude_max
    if not dark.any():
        raise ValueError(
            f"the Sun never drops below {sun_altitude_max} at {site.name} on {day.iso[:10]}"
        )

    first = int(np.argmax(dark))
    stretch = dark[first:]
    length = int(np.argmin(stretch)) if not stretch.all() else len(stretch)
    sel = slice(first, first + length)
    return Night(
        times=times[sel],
        sun_altitude=sun_alt[sel].to(u.deg),
        start=times[sel][0],
        end=times[sel][-1],
    )

Worst-case V-band light-pollution enhancement from La Serena/Coquimbo at Cerro Tololo (assumed for Cerro Pachon, ~10 km away), vs. zenith distance.

Krisciunas et al. (2007, PASP, 119, 687; arXiv:0705.1153) found no detectable effect of the towns' artificial light for elevation > 45 deg (zenith distance < 45 deg, airmass < 1.41) -- only below 45 deg elevation does La Serena's glow become measurable (visible from ~10 deg elevation). Krisciunas, Bogglio, Sanhueza & Smith (2010, PASP, 122, 373; arXiv:1001.2246) confirmed this with new data and quantified the worst case: on a clear night (no marine cloud layer over La Serena/Coquimbo), facing directly toward the town (azimuth roughly 260-310 deg in their data), V-band flux reached up to a factor of ~2 (44-72% excess) above the Garstang (1989) model near zenith distance 80 deg (airmass ~5.8); B-band showed no corresponding enhancement at all, and a similarly high zenith angle toward Andacollo (a smaller, less light-polluted town, a different azimuth) also showed none.

This returns a conservative, azimuth-independent upper bound, not a measured correction: 1.0 (no effect) below 45 deg zenith distance, linearly ramping to 2.0 by 80 deg (a simple interpolation of the two papers' own anchor points, not a physical radiative-transfer model -- kino.observing has no notion of "direction toward La Serena" to do better), held flat at 2.0 beyond 80 deg (unverified extrapolation past the papers' own data). V-band only; nothing here applies to B or other bands, where the effect was not detected. forecast_ifu/ forecast_slit's own default max_airmass=2.0 corresponds to zenith distance 60 deg -- comfortably inside the well-measured no-detectable-effect regime (<~70 deg in the 2010 data) for any forecast run at that default or lower; this function exists for the unusual case of deliberately forecasting at much higher airmass.

def la_serena_worst_case_factor(zenith_distance: u.Quantity) -> np.ndarray:

    Cerro Tololo (assumed for Cerro Pachon, ~10 km away), vs. zenith distance.

    Krisciunas et al. (2007, PASP, 119, 687; arXiv:0705.1153) found **no**
    detectable effect of the towns' artificial light for elevation > 45 deg
    (zenith distance < 45 deg, airmass < 1.41) -- only below 45 deg elevation
    does La Serena's glow become measurable (visible from ~10 deg elevation).
    Krisciunas, Bogglio, Sanhueza & Smith (2010, PASP, 122, 373;
    arXiv:1001.2246) confirmed this with new data and quantified the worst
    case: on a clear night (no marine cloud layer over La Serena/Coquimbo),
    facing directly toward the town (azimuth roughly 260-310 deg in their
    data), V-band flux reached up to a factor of ~2 (44-72% excess) above the
    Garstang (1989) model near zenith distance 80 deg (airmass ~5.8); B-band
    showed **no** corresponding enhancement at all, and a similarly high
    zenith angle toward Andacollo (a smaller, less light-polluted town, a
    different azimuth) also showed none.

    This returns a **conservative, azimuth-independent upper bound**, not a
    measured correction: 1.0 (no effect) below 45 deg zenith distance,
    linearly ramping to 2.0 by 80 deg (a simple interpolation of the two
    papers' own anchor points, not a physical radiative-transfer model --
    ``kino.observing`` has no notion of "direction toward La Serena" to do
    better), held flat at 2.0 beyond 80 deg (unverified extrapolation past
    the papers' own data). V-band only; nothing here applies to B or other
    bands, where the effect was not detected. ``forecast_ifu``/
    ``forecast_slit``'s own default ``max_airmass=2.0`` corresponds to
    zenith distance 60 deg -- comfortably inside the well-measured
    no-detectable-effect regime (<~70 deg in the 2010 data) for any forecast
    run at that default or lower; this function exists for the unusual case
    of deliberately forecasting at much higher airmass.
    """
    z = np.asarray(u.Quantity(zenith_distance).to_value(u.deg), dtype=float)
    lo, hi = 45.0, 80.0
    frac = np.clip((z - lo) / (hi - lo), 0.0, 1.0)
    return 1.0 + frac

with a the lunar phase angle (0 = full), r the Moon-target separation, Zm/Z the zenith distances of the Moon and the target. def moonlight_brightness(
    phase_angle: u.Quantity,
    separation: u.Quantity,
    moon_zenith_distance: u.Quantity,
    zenith_distance: u.Quantity,
    k: float,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Scattered moonlight in the V band, nanoLamberts (K&S91 Section 5).

    ::

        I*   = 10^(-0.4 (3.84 + 0.026|a| + 4e-9 a^4))     lunar illuminance
        f(r) = 10^5.36 (1.06 + cos^2 r) + 10^(6.15 - r/40)    r >= 10 deg
        f(r) = 10^5.36 (1.06 + cos^2 r) + 6.2e7 / r^2         r <  10 deg
        B    = f(r) I* 10^(-0.4 k X(Zm)) [1 - 10^(-0.4 k X(Z))]

    with ``a`` the lunar phase angle (0 = full), ``r`` the Moon-target
    separation, ``Zm``/``Z`` the zenith distances of the Moon and the target.
    The ``r < 10 deg`` branch is the aureole term (K&S91 eq. 19, Schaefer 1991)
    replacing the Mie term; the paper's summary formula is stated for
    r > 10 deg only. Returns 0 when the Moon is below the horizon.

    ``phase_angle``, ``separation`` and the zenith distances broadcast
    together; ``k`` is the V-band extinction (mag per airmass).
    """
    alpha = np.abs(np.asarray(u.Quantity(phase_angle).to_value(u.deg), dtype=float))
    rho = np.asarray(u.Quantity(separation).to_value(u.deg), dtype=float)
    zm = u.Quantity(moon_zenith_distance)
    z = u.Quantity(zenith_distance)

    i_star = 10.0 ** (-0.4 * (3.84 + 0.026 * alpha + 4e-9 * alpha**4))
    cos2 = np.cos(np.radians(rho)) ** 2
    rayleigh = 10.0**5.36 * (1.06 + cos2)
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
        mie = np.where(rho >= 10.0, 10.0 ** (6.15 - rho / 40.0), 6.2e7 / np.maximum(rho, 1e-6) ** 2)
    f = rayleigh + mie

    x_moon = _night_glow_airmass(zm)
    x_sky = _night_glow_airmass(z)
    b = f * i_star * 10.0 ** (-0.4 * k * x_moon) * (1.0 - 10.0 ** (-0.4 * k * x_sky))
    return np.where(np.asarray(zm.to_value(u.deg)) < 90.0, b, 0.0)

def sky_brightness_v(
    dark_zenith_mag: float,
    phase_angle: u.Quantity,
    separation: u.Quantity,
    moon_zenith_distance: u.Quantity,
    zenith_distance: u.Quantity,
    k: float,
) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Total V-band sky brightness with the Moon.

    Returns ``{"dark": nL, "moon": nL, "total": nL, "total_mag": mag/arcsec^2,
    "delta_v": mag}`` where ``delta_v = -2.5 log10(total / dark)`` is the
    brightening from moonlight (K&S91 eq. 22, negative = brighter).
    """
    dark = dark_sky_brightness(dark_zenith_mag, zenith_distance, k)
    moon = moonlight_brightness(phase_angle, separation, moon_zenith_distance, zenith_distance, k)
    total = dark + moon
    return {

        "moon": moon,
        "total": total,
        "total_mag": mag_from_nanolamberts(total),
        "delta_v": -2.5 * np.log10(total / dark),
    }

def sky_electron_rate(
    sky: SkySpectrum,
    *,
    pixel_area: u.Quantity,
    effective_area: u.Quantity,
    throughput,
) -> u.Quantity:
    """Detected sky electrons per second per pixel per channel.

    ``rate = radiance * channel_width * pixel_area * effective_area * throughput``
    -- the same collecting area and end-to-end throughput
    :func:`kino.instruments.base.photon_flux_to_electrons` applies to the
    source, so source and sky are on one footing. ``throughput`` is a
    :class:`~kino.instruments.base.Throughput`, evaluated at the channel
    centres. Suitable as ``IFU.sky_electron_rate`` (which multiplies by the
    total exposure time itself).
    """
    radiance = sky.total * (u.photon / u.s / u.m**2 / u.um / u.arcsec**2)

docs.title: kino.observing.skymodel
docs.text:
Night-sky radiance spectra from a local library of ESO SkyCalc output.

SkyLibrary interpolates, offline, spectra of the four sky components that matter at optical wavelengths -- scattered moonlight, airglow (emission lines plus residual continuum), zodiacal light and scattered starlight -- computed with ESO's Cerro Paranal Advanced Sky Model (Noll et al. 2012, A&A 543, A92; Jones et al. 2013, A&A 560, A91). The library is built once from the SkyCalc service by scripts/build_skycalc_library.py (network, ~10 minutes) and kept in data/skycalc/ (git-ignored), so batch runs are offline and reproducible.

Radiance is in photons / s / m^2 / micron / arcsec^2 at the ground (it already includes the sky's own extinction); wavelengths are vacuum, in nm.

What was checked against independent references (V band, see the tests and CLAUDE.md): the dark zenith sky is 21.9 mag/arcsec^2 at 100 s.f.u. against the CTIO mean 21.79 +/- 0.22 (Krisciunas et al. 2007), and the moonlight brightening agrees with Krisciunas & Schaefer (1991) to 0.1-0.4 mag across four geometries.

Approximations and known limits -- read before trusting a number:

  • the model is for Cerro Paranal (2640 m); Cerro Pachon (SOAR/Gemini South) has more water vapour (irrelevant below ~1 micron), different aerosols, and La Serena's light pollution at low elevation, none of which is modelled;
  • airglow is averaged over seasons and the whole night, although it varies by tens of percent within a night; it scales with the 10.7 cm solar flux, which the caller must supply for the epoch (there is no default you can trust);
  • moonlight is interpolated (log-linear) on a grid in phase, target-Moon separation, Moon zenith distance and airmass, capped at airmass 2 and at a Moon zenith distance of 80 deg with a linear taper to zero at the horizon;
  • zodiacal light and starlight are stored at airmass 1 and scaled by the CTIO extinction curve; the ecliptic longitude is measured relative to the Sun and differs by ~4 deg from SkyCalc's own almanac for one tested target, which matters little far from the Sun;
  • wavelengths are vacuum -- convert if you compare sky lines with air wavelengths.

def __init__(self, moon: dict, airglow: dict, zodi: dict, meta: dict | None = None):
    self.meta = meta or {}
    self._moon_lam = np.asarray(moon["lam_nm"], dtype=float)
    self._moon_axes = (
        np.asarray(moon["elongation"], dtype=float),
        np.asarray(moon["target_sep"], dtype=float),
        np.asarray(moon["zenith_dist_moon"], dtype=float),
        np.asarray(moon["airmass"], dtype=float),
    )

        self._moon_axes,
        np.log10(np.maximum(np.asarray(moon["radiance"], dtype=float), 1e-6)),
        bounds_error=False,
        fill_value=None,
    )
    self._glow_lam = np.asarray(airglow["lam_nm"], dtype=float)
    self._glow = RegularGridInterpolator(
        (
            np.asarray(airglow["airmass"], dtype=float),
            np.asarray(airglow["solar_flux"], dtype=float),
        ),
        np.asarray(airglow["radiance"], dtype=float),
        bounds_error=False,
        fill_value=None,
    )
    self._zodi_lam = np.asarray(zodi["lam_nm"], dtype=float)
    self._zodi = RegularGridInterpolator(

        bounds_error=False,

def spectrum(self, conditions: SkyConditions, wavelength_edges: u.Quantity) -> SkySpectrum:
    """Sky components averaged over the channels bounded by ``wavelength_edges``.

    ``wavelength_edges`` are *vacuum* wavelengths, shape ``(n + 1,)``.
    """
    if conditions.airmass < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("airmass must be >= 1")
    edges_nm = u.Quantity(wavelength_edges).to_value(u.nm)
    if edges_nm[0] < _MIN_LAMBDA_NM:
        raise ValueError(f"the sky model is used above {_MIN_LAMBDA_NM:.0f} nm")
    return SkySpectrum(
        wavelength_edges=u.Quantity(wavelength_edges).to(u.nm),
        components={
            "moon": bin_to_channels(self._moon_lam, self.moonlight(conditions), edges_nm),
            "airglow": bin_to_channels(self._glow_lam, self.airglow(conditions), edges_nm),
            "zodiacal": bin_to_channels(self._zodi_lam, self.zodiacal(conditions), edges_nm),
            "starlight": bin_to_channels(self._zodi_lam, self.starlight(conditions), edges_nm),
        },
    )

docs.title: bin_to_channels(lam_nm: np.ndarray, radiance: np.ndarray, edges_nm: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
docs.text:
Mean of radiance(lam) over each channel [edges[i], edges[i+1]].

Integrates the piecewise-linear spectrum exactly via its cumulative integral, so narrow sky lines contribute their true flux to a wide channel instead of being sampled or missed. Channels partly outside the library range are averaged over the covered part; fully outside raises.

Source code in kino/observing/skymodel.py 
def bin_to_channels(lam_nm: np.ndarray, radiance: np.ndarray, edges_nm: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Mean of ``radiance(lam)`` over each channel ``[edges[i], edges[i+1]]``.

    Integrates the piecewise-linear spectrum exactly via its cumulative
    integral, so narrow sky lines contribute their true flux to a wide channel
    instead of being sampled or missed. Channels partly outside the library
    range are averaged over the covered part; fully outside raises.
    """
    edges = np.asarray(edges_nm, dtype=float)
    if edges[0] < lam_nm[0] or edges[-1] > lam_nm[-1]:
        raise ValueError(
            f"channels {edges[0]:.1f}-{edges[-1]:.1f} nm extend outside the sky library "
            f"({lam_nm[0]:.1f}-{lam_nm[-1]:.1f} nm)"
        )
    cum = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(0.5 * (radiance[1:] + radiance[:-1]) * np.diff(lam_nm))])
    at_edges = np.interp(edges, lam_nm, cum)
    return np.diff(at_edges) / np.diff(edges)

docs.title: Adding an instrument config
docs.text: Every config in kino/config/ is a plain YAML file loaded with IFU.from_config(path) or SlitSpectrograph.from_config(path) (kino.instruments.config does the parsing). This page is the recipe used to build keck_kcwi.yaml, gemini_gmos_ifu.yaml, vlt_muse.yaml, and the AO-fed gemini_nifs.yaml/keck_osiris.yaml, and it generalizes to any new IFU or slit spectrograph.

docs.title: The fields a config needs
docs.text:
pixel_scale: "0.20 arcsec"      # spatial sampling
nx: 50                          # spaxels across
ny: 50                          # spaxels along

wavelength_min: "0.6950 um"     # spectral window (narrow it for speed; see below)
wavelength_max: "0.7050 um"
n_wave: 80                      # channel count -> sets the per-channel dispersion

lsf:
  fwhm: "2.333 angstrom"        # Gaussian line-spread function

psf:
  seeing_fwhm: "0.74 arcsec"    # combined with aperture_diameter for the optical PSF

throughput:
  wavelength: ["0.480 um", "0.750 um", "0.930 um"]
  transmission: [0.14, 0.35, 0.14]

aperture_diameter: "8.2 m"
obstruction_fraction: 0.013     # 0.0 if your aperture is already obstruction-corrected

detector:
  read_noise: "3.0 electron"
  dark_current: "0.0005 electron / s"

exposure_time: "1200 s"
n_exposures: 3

sky_electron_rate: "0 electron / s"  # per spaxel, already-detected rate (not a sky brightness)

Every physical quantity is a string astropy.units.Quantity can parse. PSF also accepts optical-aberration keys (defocus, astig1, astig2, coma1, coma2, trefoil1, trefoil2, spher) for an AO-fed instrument — none of the configs shipped so far use them (all default to zero, unaberrated optics).

AO-fed instruments (gemini_nifs.yaml, keck_osiris.yaml) still only set seeing_fwhm, not the aberration keys. KINO has no dedicated Strehl-ratio or core+halo AO PSF model, so both configs plug the instrument's own quoted (NIFS) or computed-diffraction-limit (OSIRIS) AO-corrected FWHM directly into seeing_fwhm as an effective single-Gaussian-equivalent width. This is a documented approximation: a real AO PSF has a near-diffraction-limited core atop an extended seeing-like halo, so this understates flux lost to the halo and makes AO forecasts optimistic until KINO gets a real AO PSF model. Follow the same pattern for any future AO-fed config rather than inventing a different convention.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Find real numbers where they're published. Start from the instrument's own characteristics page: field of view and spatial sampling, grating/grism resolving power and wavelength coverage, detector pixel size, telescope aperture. These are usually the easiest to find and the least likely to need a fiducial.

  2. Throughput is almost always the hard part. In rough order of preference:

    • A real on-sky measurement, the way scripts/derive_goodman_throughput.py derives Goodman's own curve from a NOIRLab exposure of a spectrophotometric standard star — the strongest option, but needs a real calibration frame to exist and be found.
    • A public exposure-time calculator's own quoted throughput (Gemini's ITC, ESO's ETC): vlt_muse.yaml's curve is exactly this — ESO's own MUSE overview page states 14%/35%/14% at 480/750/930 nm, used unmodified, no interpolation invented.
    • A clearly-labelled fiducial shape anchored to one real peak-efficiency number from the instrument paper (keck_kcwi.yaml does this: a bell curve peaking at the literature's own "in excess of 45%" figure).

  3. Never leave a config blocked on a missing number. If detector read noise, dark current, or sky background aren't published, search for a defensible fiducial (a cross-instrument proxy from the same detector family, a typical value for that class of detector) rather than leaving the config unusable. Every placeholder number lives in the file's own header comment, explicitly labelled UNVERIFIED/PLACEHOLDER, with either its source or the reasoning behind the fiducial — never a silently-assumed number. A working config with labelled fiducials ships; a blocked one doesn't, and real users will want to override these values themselves, which only works if the config loads in the first place.

  4. Keep the spectral/spatial window small by default. A real instrument's full field or wavelength range is often far larger than any single target needs (MUSE's real WFM field is 60″×60″; the shipped config crops it to 10″×10″ for rendering speed) and makes every render needlessly slow. Document the crop in the header and tell users how to override it for the real full field/range.

  5. Pin every sourced number with a test. One test file per config, mirroring tests/instruments/test_goodman_config.py: assert the geometry, detector, LSF, and throughput match what the header claims, and pin the fact that any placeholder is still a placeholder (so replacing it later is a deliberate, visible test change, not a silent pass). Finish with one real ifu.observe(...) call asserting a finite, non-trivial cube — confirms the config actually forecasts something sane, not just that the YAML parses.

  6. Cite everything in the header. Every sourced number says where it came from (a URL, a paper with its full citation, an instrument manual section); every placeholder says why it's a placeholder and what a real value would need. This is what makes a config trustworthy enough to build a real proposal's forecast on top of — which is exactly what sifs.yaml/goodman.yaml were used for.

docs.title: Batch mock generation
docs.text: A single mock (docs/quickstart.md) is a galaxy, a shear, and an instrument. A catalogue generalizes this to many galaxies at once, sharing one instrument and one global reduced shear -- KINO treats shear this way everywhere (every forecast/notebook assumes a single (g1, g2) per target); a spatially-varying shear field is out of scope.

docs.title: A minimal catalogue
docs.text:
instrument:
  kind: ifu                        # "ifu" or "slit"
  config: kino/config/sifs.yaml

shear:
  g1: 0.03
  g2: -0.01

seed: 42

galaxies:
  - r_e: 0.5
    inc: 60
    pa: 30
    v_flat: 180
    z: 0.10
    sigma0: 30
    line_flux: "1.0e-15 erg / (s cm2)"
    line_wavelength: "0.65628 um"
  - r_e: 0.8
    inc: 45
    pa: 10
    v_flat: 220
    z: 0.15
    sigma0: 35
    line_flux: "5.0e-15 erg / (s cm2)"
    line_wavelength: "0.65628 um"

from kino.mocks.catalogue import generate_batch

paths = generate_batch("catalogue.yaml", "mock_batch/", format="fits")

or from the shell:

python examples/generate_catalogue.py --catalogue catalogue.yaml --out mock_batch/

This writes mock_batch/galaxy_0000.fits, galaxy_0001.fits, ... plus mock_batch/manifest.json recording each galaxy's true parameters, its output filename, and the per-galaxy noise seed used.

Every key in a galaxy row must be a kino.galaxy.DiscGalaxy constructor field (r_e, inc, pa, v_flat are required; everything else defaults as DiscGalaxy itself documents) plus the two observation-level extras line_flux/line_wavelength -- both parsed the same way every instrument config parses a physical value ("<value> <unit>"). An unknown key raises ValueError naming the allowed set, so a typo is caught immediately rather than silently ignored.

docs.title: Sampling a population instead of listing galaxies
docs.text:
Replace galaxies: with population: to draw n galaxies from per-field distributions instead of listing them:

population:
  n: 50
  r_e: {dist: uniform, low: 0.3, high: 1.0}
  inc: {dist: uniform, low: 20, high: 80}
  pa: {dist: uniform, low: 0, high: 180}
  v_flat: {dist: lognormal, median: 180, scatter_dex: 0.1}
  z: {dist: uniform, low: 0.05, high: 0.5}
  sigma0: {dist: uniform, low: 20, high: 40}
  line_flux: {dist: loguniform, low: 1.0e-16, high: 1.0e-14, unit: "erg / (s cm2)"}
  line_wavelength: "0.65628 um"       # a bare scalar is fixed for every galaxy

Three distributions are supported -- deliberately a small, fixed set, not a general DSL:

  • uniform: low, high.
  • loguniform: low, high (both must be positive).
  • lognormal: median, scatter_dex (log10 scatter -- the same convention kino.inference.priors.tully_fisher_prior uses).

A DiscGalaxy field (r_e, inc, ...) samples a plain number directly. line_flux/line_wavelength are astropy.units.Quantity-valued, so a sampled value for either needs an explicit unit: key (appended to the drawn number before parsing) -- see line_flux above.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Exactly one of galaxies/population must be set, and the catalogue's one top-level seed is spawned into n + 1 independent numpy.random.SeedSequence children: one seeds the population sampler (unused for an explicit list), and one seeds each galaxy's noise realisation -- the same pattern kino.analysis.injection uses internally. Running generate_batch twice on the same catalogue file therefore regenerates byte-identical output files and an identical manifest.json, whether the galaxies are listed or sampled.

docs.title: Reading a batch back
docs.text:
Each file is a normal kino.io.fitsio/kino.io.hdf5 product (pick the format with generate_batch(..., format="fits" | "hdf5")), with every galaxy/shear/line parameter recorded in its own Datacube.meta by kino.mocks.single.simulate_observation -- the same mechanism examples/simulate_one_galaxy.py + run_inference.py use to round-trip truth values without a bespoke header:

from kino.io import fitsio

cube = fitsio.read_datacube("mock_batch/galaxy_0000.fits")
print(cube.meta["r_e"], cube.meta["g1"], cube.meta["line_flux"])

manifest.json holds the same information for every galaxy in one file, so a downstream script (an ensemble inference run, say) doesn't need to open every data file just to check the truth it's recovering.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: Every module in KINO follows the same units and sign conventions. Getting one of these backwards (a shear sign, a PA direction, an ellipticity definition) produces a plausible, wrong answer rather than an obvious crash — read this page before writing code that touches angles, signs, or shear.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• Positions: arcsec, origin at the galaxy centroid.
  • Velocities: km/s.
  • Wavelengths: µm internally; Å or nm at public API boundaries where that's the field's own convention (config files, spectra).
  • Angles: degrees.
  • All public API boundaries use astropy.units explicitly — if a function takes a bare float where you'd expect a Quantity, check its docstring for which unit it assumes.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text: Image-plane Cartesian (x, y) in arcsec, origin at the galaxy centroid; x increases to the East, y to the North.

docs.title: Position angle (PA)
docs.text: Degrees, East of North, of the disc's major axis.

docs.title: Inclination
docs.text: i = 0 is face-on, i = 90° is edge-on.

docs.title: Ellipticity & shear
docs.text: Reduced shear g = g1 + i·g2 (complex), paired with the distortion/ellipticity convention ε = (a−b)/(a+b). If you ever need the χ = (a²−b²)/(a²+b²) convention instead, convert explicitly and label it — don't assume the two are interchangeable.

docs.title: Line-of-sight velocity
docs.text:
Vlos = Vsys + Vrot(r) · sin(i) · cos(θ)

in the disc frame, θ measured from the major axis. Positive Vlos means redshifted (receding). This sign convention is kept consistent between the forward model and every likelihood — a common bug when extending KINO is shearing only the morphology and forgetting the velocity field needs the same shear transform (apply_shear already handles this correctly; see its docstring for the delensing transform both quantities share).

docs.title: Cosmology
docs.text: astropy.cosmology.Planck18 is the default everywhere, always injectable — KINO never hard-codes a numeric distance.

docs.title: Randomness
docs.text: Every stochastic call takes an explicit, seeded numpy.random.Generator. KINO never reads the global np.random state — this is what makes a run (a config + a seed) exactly reproducible.

docs.title: Shear is applied to the image and the velocity field
docs.text: A disc galaxy's surface brightness and its line-of-sight velocity field are both remapped through the identical delensing transform (kino.lensing.scene.LensedScene/apply_shear) — shear is never applied to the morphology alone. This is the single most important invariant in the forward model: a shear measurement that only distorted the image shape would be measuring something else entirely.

docs.title: Instrument flux calibration
docs.text: A DiscGalaxy's flux (and anything derived from it, like a LensedScene's surface brightness) is in the galaxy's own arbitrary units — KINO is intentionally unitless there. Physical calibration happens at Instrument.observe() time: pass an explicit line_flux (astropy.units.Quantity, e.g. erg/s/cm**2) and the renderer rescales the shape by line_flux / galaxy.flux. Because a LensedScene is evaluated by sampling the unlensed galaxy at each observed (delensed) sky position, the image-integrated flux comes out magnified relative to galaxy.flux automatically — line_flux is always the source's intrinsic, unlensed brightness; never re-apply magnification on top of it.

docs.title: Noise and sky background
docs.text: Instrument backends return detected electrons, combining Poisson source/sky/dark-current shot noise with Gaussian read noise. rng=None returns the noiseless expected-count cube instead of drawing a noise realisation — useful for inspecting the pure signal. Sky background (sky_electron_rate) is specified already as a detected electron rate (as an observatory's own exposure-time calculator would give it), not a sky surface brightness — it does not go through the source's own throughput/aperture pipeline.

docs.title: Forecasting a target
docs.text:
This is the same workflow behind KINO's own real telescope-time proposals — going from a target's coordinates and line flux to a shear S/N forecast through a real night at a real site. The numbers below are a synthetic, illustrative target, not a real one (candidate target lists are private — see CLAUDE.md).

import numpy as np
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from kino.galaxy import DiscGalaxy
from kino.instruments.ifu import IFU
from kino.analysis.forecast import ForecastTarget, forecast_ifu
from kino.observing import SOAR, night_window, SkyLibrary, solar_flux

gal = DiscGalaxy(r_e=1.2, inc=55.0, pa=30.0, v_flat=180.0, z=0.45, sigma0=40.0)
coord = SkyCoord(ra=150.0 * u.deg, dec=2.5 * u.deg)
target = ForecastTarget(
    coord, gal, 1e-15 * u.erg / u.s / u.cm**2, "OII3727", name="demo"
)

ifu = IFU.from_config("kino/config/sifs.yaml")
lib = SkyLibrary.load("data/skycalc")        # needs the `sky` extra's data, see Install
night = night_window(SOAR, "2027-06-15")
F107 = solar_flux("2027-06")[0]              # monthly-mean 10.7cm solar flux

forecast = forecast_ifu(
    ifu, target, night, lib,
    g=(0.03, -0.01),
    seeing_ref=[1.0] * u.arcsec,
    solar_flux=F107,
    time_step=60 * u.min,
    max_airmass=2.0,
    window_kms=350.0,
)
print("shear S/N:", np.nanmax(forecast.shear_snr_stat[:, 0]))

docs.title: The window_kms gotcha
docs.text:
Don't drop window_kms=350.0 from that call — it matters more than it looks. forecast_ifu/forecast_slit default to window_kms=500.0, a spectral half-width wider than most emission lines actually need. The per-spaxel detection gate inside shear_fisher's cube estimator aborts the entire calculation (returning an undetectable result, not just a worse one) if literally zero spaxels individually clear snr_threshold — and a too-wide window adds pure-noise channels that push marginal spaxels below that threshold sooner, especially at low exposure time or poor seeing, long before the shear information itself is actually lost.

This produced a real false "seeing cliff" in an early draft of KINO's own SOAR proposal — a sharp, physically implausible dropout that very nearly shipped as a stated hard requirement before it was traced to this exact mechanism. Pick window_kms from the line's own real extent instead of trusting the default: render the model with rng=None and measure how much flux actually falls within a candidate half-width before committing to it (kino.analysis.moments.crop_to_line does this cropping once you know the right value). This is a known pipeline sharp edge, not fixed at the gate level yet — treat the default as a starting point to check, not a safe choice.

docs.title: Scanning a whole night, or a whole semester
docs.text:
forecast_ifu/forecast_slit already tile (time, seeing) through one night for you (that's what the loop over night.times inside them does). To scan multiple candidate nights across a semester — and, for a real proposal, to rank several candidate targets against each other — kino.analysis.semester loops the per-night forecast for you:

from kino.analysis.semester import semester_dates, forecast_over_nights, rank_candidates

dates = semester_dates("2027-05-01", "2027-11-30", step_days=7)  # weekly stride

nightly = forecast_over_nights(
    ifu, target, dates, lib,
    g=(0.03, -0.01), seeing_ref=[1.0] * u.arcsec, site=SOAR, time_step=180 * u.min,
)
print(nightly.summary())   # the single best night across the whole range

# several candidates (never commit a real target list -- see CLAUDE.md), ranked:
ranked = rank_candidates(ifu, [target_a, target_b, target_c], dates, lib, g=(0.03, -0.01),
                          seeing_ref=[1.0] * u.arcsec, site=SOAR)

Each night collapses to its single best (time, seeing) point (not the full grid) and the right month's solar flux is looked up for you — pass solar_flux_fn to cover dates outside the tabulated NOAA months. Keep seeing_ref to one or two values and step_days/time_step coarse for an exploratory scan across many nights or candidates; this is still the same per-point shear_fisher cost as a single-night forecast, multiplied by every date and target, so a full semester at a fine grid is slow (see the module's own docstring for the cost trade-off).

docs.title: IFU vs. slit
docs.text: forecast_ifu takes an IFU; forecast_slit takes a SlitSpectrograph and additionally models slit losses and misalignment directly in the render (not as a separate correction factor) — swap the instrument and the function, keep everything else the same. See Adding an instrument config for how either kind of config is built.

docs.title: Running inference
docs.text:
The Quickstart's shear_fisher call gives a fast Cramér–Rao bound on shear precision. To actually recover a (g1, g2) posterior from mock (or real) data, fit a likelihood with nested sampling. This is the real pattern notebooks/04_one_galaxy_inference.ipynb runs end to end — reuse it rather than re-deriving one, since nested sampling through the full cube likelihood takes real time (minutes, not seconds; budget accordingly, and prefer running it as a script or notebook rather than inline in a REPL).

from kino.inference.likelihood import IFUCubeLikelihood
from kino.inference.priors import build_prior, tully_fisher_prior
from kino.inference.sampler import fit_shear

# Everything the likelihood should treat as *fixed* (known from imaging/
# redshift), as opposed to free parameters fit from the data cube itself.
fixed_galaxy_params = {
    "r_e": gal.r_e,
    "pa": gal.pa,
    "z": gal.z,
    "sigma0": gal.sigma0,
    "flux": gal.flux,
}

likelihood = IFUCubeLikelihood(
    ifu=ifu,
    line_wavelength=line_wavelength,
    data=data,                       # the observed (or mock) Datacube
    fixed_galaxy_params=fixed_galaxy_params,
    fixed_line_flux=line_flux,
)

# Free parameters and their priors. g1/g2/line_flux are handled by the
# likelihood itself and must NOT be passed as DiscGalaxy fields; any other
# free parameter must be a real DiscGalaxy field.
prior = build_prior(
    {
        "g1": (-0.15, 0.15),
        "g2": (-0.15, 0.15),
        "inc": (30.0, 80.0),
        "v_flat": tully_fisher_prior(gal.flux, v0=180.0, flux0=1.0, scatter_dex=0.15),
    }
)

posterior = fit_shear(prior, likelihood, n_live=150, seed=0, n_eff=300)

posterior.samples holds equal-weighted posterior samples (columns in prior order), and posterior.log_z the Bayesian evidence. nautilus (neural-network-boosted importance nested sampling) is KINO's sole sampler — see CLAUDE.md's "Language / stack" convention for why.

docs.title: Which likelihood?
docs.text:
Three are available (kino.inference.likelihood), sharing one forward model:

Likelihood Instrument Notes IFUCubeLikelihood IFU Voxel-level; the one to use for an IFU. SlitCubeLikelihood SlitSpectrograph Voxel-level; fits SlitObservation.spectrum only — the companion broadband image is a placement aid, never fit. IFUMomentLikelihood IFU Compares flux/Vlos/dispersion moment maps instead of the raw cube. Kept for comparison only — it has a real noise bias at low S/N (see its own docstring). Prefer IFUCubeLikelihood for an actual shear measurement.

All three forward-model each trial through the same instrument .observe(..., rng=None) used for the data — never compare a rendered cube against an analytically-evaluated model, or the fit is biased by exactly the PSF/LSF beam-smearing amount.

docs.title: Sanity-check before sampling
docs.text:
Nested sampling is expensive; check the likelihood is sane first by evaluating it directly at the injected truth and slightly off it — the truth should score higher:

ll_truth = likelihood({"inc": gal.inc, "v_flat": gal.v_flat, "g1": g1_true, "g2": g2_true})
ll_off = likelihood({"inc": gal.inc, "v_flat": gal.v_flat, "g1": g1_true + 0.05, "g2": g2_true})
assert ll_truth > ll_off
